column1: # perf/wasm_baselines.tsv — wall-time budgets for the wasm32-wasip1
# build under wasmtime. Sibling to `baselines.tsv` (which gates
# native rubyrs); same absolute-baseline policy + ratchet etiquette,
# scoped to the wasi shape because wasmtime startup + JIT + wasi
# syscall costs make native budgets irrelevant here.
# Format (tab-separated):
#   <workload-path>\t<max_wall_ms>\t<note>
# Only wall-time is gated. Peak-RSS isn't meaningful under wasmtime —
# the guest's linear memory is hidden behind a host VM and the
# `/usr/bin/time` numbers conflate wasmtime's runtime overhead
# with the guest's working set; without a stable lever there is
# no useful ratchet.
# Bumping etiquette: same as `baselines.tsv` — bump with a comment
# above the row explaining what grew and whether it was intentional;
# never "bumped to make CI green" silently.
# What the gate actually measures
# `perf/wasm_check.sh` builds a `.cwasm` ahead of time (raw .wasm →
# wasm-opt -Oz → `wasmtime compile`) and times each workload via
# `wasmtime run --allow-precompiled $CWASM`. There is no per-run
# JIT step — the cwasm carries pre-JIT'd machine code — so the
# `~/.cache/wasmtime` warm-up cycle that affected raw-.wasm
# measurements no longer applies; every one of the 3 timed runs
# is essentially the same shape (load .cwasm + run script).
# MIN-of-3 (same reducer as host `baselines.tsv`) is still useful
# despite that: it filters CI spawn jitter, OS page-cache warm-up
# of the .cwasm file itself, `/usr/bin/time`'s 10 ms-granularity
# rounding, and other host-level noise that the JIT-elimination
# can't address.
# The regression signal we want is "did the rubyrs interpreter
# get slower under wasi". Pre-compiling to .cwasm isolates that
# from wasmtime's own JIT cost; min-of-3 then strips spawn
# jitter from the resulting wall.
# Initial calibration (Apple M-series, wasmtime 45.0.0,
# rubyrs.wasm release build, wasm-opt -Oz + wasmtime compile AOT,
# MIN of 3 runs each):
#   startup_floor.rb   ~7-10 ms (sub-`/usr/bin/time` granularity;
#                                first run is now flat — no JIT
#                                step in the wasmtime path because
#                                we measure against the .cwasm).
#   brewfile_dsl.rb    ~10 ms   (P2-A pivot workload — ~50 method
#                                calls, class def, `.each` loops,
#                                still sub-granularity).
#   fizzbuzz_1m.rb     ~510 ms.
# AOT-compiled `.cwasm` means the `startup_floor` story compares
# favourably to native rubyrs (~2 ms) AND wins against MRI
# (`ruby --yjit` cold start ~80 ms on the same Mac). The wall
# the gate measures is now end-to-end "wasmtime spawn + load
# precompiled module + run script", with no per-run JIT cost.
# CI is on ubuntu-latest x86_64, where wasmtime + wasi-portable
# code typically run 1.5-2× slower than Apple Silicon native.
# Budgets below sit at ~10× the local M-series observed wall —
# the headroom is bigger than the native `baselines.tsv`'s ~2×
# because the startup_floor budget is now much smaller (single-
# digit ms) where measurement granularity + spawn jitter
# dominate; absolute ms headroom matters more than the ratio.
# Expect a re-cal commit if/when the wasmtime version pinned in
# CI bumps or the wasi-sdk shape changes.
